mcqs.question: Why does sorting intervals by start time make a single left-to-right pass sufficient to merge them?
options: Because once starts only increase, no later interval can overlap anything except the current merge — everything earlier has already been resolved
Because sorting removes all duplicate intervals before the merge begins
Because sorted intervals are guaranteed to already be non-overlapping
Because the sort reduces the number of intervals that need to be compared to a constant
mcqs.explanation: With starts in non-decreasing order, any interval that could still overlap the current merge must be the next one in line — nothing later can sneak in without first overlapping something already scanned. Sorting doesn't dedupe or pre-merge anything; it just orders the input so one pass suffices.

mcqs.question: Given `[1,10], [2,3], [4,5]` sorted by start, what goes wrong if you compare each new interval against the previous *input* interval instead of the last *merged* result?
options: The algorithm crashes because the previous input interval is undefined at the first step
`[4,5]` gets compared against `[2,3]`, wrongly looks disjoint from it, and gets emitted as a spurious extra interval instead of being absorbed into `[1,10]`
The final output has too few intervals because everything gets merged into one
The sort order gets corrupted, causing intervals to be processed out of order
mcqs.explanation: `[2,3]` is the previous input interval but `[1,10]` is the actual last merged range once `[2,3]` gets absorbed into it. Comparing `[4,5]` against the stale `[2,3]` instead of `[1,10]` misses that it should also be absorbed, producing an incorrect extra interval in the output.

mcqs.question: `[1,2]` and `[2,3]` share only the single point 2. How should you decide whether to merge them?
options: Always merge them — touching intervals are overlapping by definition in every problem
Never merge them — a shared endpoint never counts as an overlap
It depends on the problem's stated convention, and that choice determines whether you use `<=` or `<` in the comparison
Merge them only if the intervals contain integers rather than floating-point bounds
mcqs.explanation: Whether touching counts as overlapping is a convention the problem sets, not a universal rule — calendar-style coverage problems typically merge touching ranges (`<=`), while half-open range representations often keep them separate (`<`). There's no single correct answer independent of the problem statement.

mcqs.question: Merge Intervals runs in O(n log n). If the interviewer says the input is guaranteed to already arrive sorted by start time, what changes?
options: Nothing — the merge pass itself is already O(n log n) regardless of input order
The complexity becomes O(n), since the sort — the only super-linear part — is no longer needed
The complexity becomes O(log n), since sorting was the dominant cost
The complexity is unaffected because the merge and sort must always run together
mcqs.explanation: The O(n log n) bound comes entirely from the sort; the scan itself is a single O(n) pass with constant work per interval. Remove the need to sort and the whole algorithm drops to O(n) — recognizing this shows you understand where the log n factor actually lives.

mcqs.question: Insert Interval takes an already-merged, sorted list plus one new interval. Why is it O(n) instead of the O(n log n) that Merge Intervals needs?
options: Because the existing list is already sorted, so there's nothing to sort — only one linear pass is required to place the new interval
Because Insert Interval only ever touches a constant number of existing intervals
Because Insert Interval is allowed to skip checking for overlaps entirely
Because the new interval is always inserted at the end of the list, avoiding a search
mcqs.explanation: The input to Insert Interval is already merged and sorted, so the O(n log n) sort that Merge Intervals pays for is unnecessary here — one linear scan splitting the list into before/overlapping/after zones is enough. It's not a constant-touch operation, and overlap checking is exactly what the pass does.

mcqs.question: An interviewer asks how Merge Intervals would need to change if new intervals kept arriving continuously instead of all at once. What's the senior-level answer?
options: No change is needed — the same sort-and-scan algorithm handles streaming input just as well
Merging is inherently a batch operation that needs the full input up front, so a streaming version needs a different approach — incremental insertion, periodic re-merging, or an interval tree
Streaming input can only be handled by switching from arrays to linked lists
The algorithm would need to run in O(n²) time to handle intervals arriving one at a time
mcqs.explanation: You can't know an interval is fully resolved until you've seen everything that might still extend it, which is fundamentally a batch property. Handling continuous arrivals means reaching for Insert Interval applied incrementally, periodic batch re-merges, or a dedicated data structure like an interval tree — not just rerunning the same pass.
